name: Chocho de Santa Catarina Ocotlán
confidence_why: 3 independent first-hand descriptions agree (0 state the same rule, 2 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_citation: Mock, Carol. 1977. Chocho de Santa Catarina Ocotlán, Oaxaca. Archivo de Lenguas Indígenas de México 4. México: El Colegio de México.
catalog_quote: Acento. Cada palabra tiene una sílaba tónica, generalmente la penúltima, en cuyo caso no la marcamos en la ortografía. Cuando el acento cae en otra sílaba, se marca con /ˈ/ ante la sílaba acentuada. acento en la penúltima: kąθē 'palma' ... acento final: kàˈnià 'petate'

new_statements.quote: Acento. Cada palabra tiene una sílaba tónica, generalmente la penúltima, en cuyo caso no la marcamos en la ortografía. Cuando el acento cae en otra sílaba, se marca con ' ante la sílaba acentuada. acento en la penúltima: [ka.e] 'palma'; acento final: [ka'nia] 'petate'. [p. 28:] Las vocales sencillas /i e ɛ a ɔ o u ɨ/ se alargan en sílaba tónica final de palabra o ante consonante débil /b d g z ž r l/.
new_statements.translation: Accent. Every word has one stressed syllable, generally the penultimate, in which case we do not mark it in the orthography. When the accent falls on another syllable, it is marked with ' before the stressed syllable. penultimate accent: 'palm'; final accent: 'reed mat'. [p. 28:] The simple vowels lengthen in a word-final stressed syllable or before a weak consonant.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: extracted text page 23 (printed p. 25): 'Acento / Cada palabra tiene una silaba tOnica, generalmente la penultima, en cuyo caso no la marcamos en la ortografia. Cuando el acento cae en otra silaba, se marca con,',' ante la silaba acentuada. / acento en la peratima' kaee 'palm* / acento final: ka*nie 'petate' — the Spanish matches the quote with accents restored; the Chocho forms are scanned-garbled as the compiler said. The same page lists six 'Tonos': alto, medio, bajo, alto descendente, medio ascendente, bajo ascendente. Page 26 (printed p. 28), item 5: 'Las vocales sencillas /i e ɛ a ɔ o u ɨ/ se alargan en silaba tonica final de palabra o ante consonante debil /b d g z ž r l/' — confirme…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog's penultimate rule (penultimate stress) for the default case; refines it by stating that stress is only 'generally' penultimate, that final-stressed words occur and are lexically marked, and that the language is simultaneously tonal (six tones). This source is the 1977 Archivo de Lenguas Indígenas volume for the very same town as the catalog entry, found on archive.org (ERIC) while searching for the listed works; it is offered as an additional open source, not as one of the three assigned works.
new_statements.rule_in_words: One stressed syllable per word, by default the penult; a minority of words are stressed on the final syllable and these are marked lexically in the orthography with a preceding apostrophe. The language also has six lexical tones (high, mid, low, high-falling, mid-rising, low-rising) listed on the same page, so stress coexists with tone.
new_statements.exceptions: Final-stressed words exist and are orthographically marked (example 'petate'); the p. 28 rule that simple vowels lengthen in a word-final stressed syllable confirms final stress is a real position.
new_statements.identity_note: Veerman-Leichsenring 2000 and the extra 1977 Archivo volume describe the Santa Catarina Ocotlán variety (the catalog's entry). Grosser Lerner 2000 describes Chocho of Santa María Nativitas, Coixtlahuaca, a different town's variety; d'Ascanio 2012 is a state-of-knowledge survey of Chocho in general, not tied to one town.

new_statements.quote: 5. Accent tonique — Dans les mots de deux syllabes ou plus, l’accent tonique tombe en règle générale sur la penultième. Lorsque celle-ci comporte une voyelle longue, l’accent tombe sur elle ; si la voyelle est simple, l’accent se traduit par la gémination de la consonne suivante : si2ne2 “jaune” se prononce [si1nne2]. [...] L’accent tonique a une influence sur la variation tonale (cf. § 1.3). || (p. 24) D’un point de vue auditif, le ton haut est plus prononcé que le moyen et le bas, et coïncide très souvent avec l’accent tonique ; lorsque celui-ci se déplace, le ton baisse || L’accent tonique tombant en règle générale sur la pénultième, celui-ci se déplace suite à l’ajout du possessif || S’agissant d’enclitiques, l’accent tonique ne tombe jamais sur eux.
new_statements.translation: 5. Stress — In words of two or more syllables, the stress falls as a general rule on the penultimate syllable. When that syllable contains a long vowel, the stress falls on it; if the vowel is short, the stress is realized as gemination of the following consonant: si2ne2 'yellow' is pronounced [si1nne2]. [...] Stress has an influence on tonal variation (cf. §1.3). || (p. 24) Auditorily, the high tone is more salient than mid and low, and very often coincides with the stress; when the stress moves, the tone lowers || Since stress as a rule falls on the penult, it moves when the possessive suffix is added || Being enclitics, [the coreferential pronouns] never receive the stress.
new_statements.citation: d'Ascanio, Davide. 2012. État des connaissances sur le chocho, suivi d'une étude bibliographique. Mémoire (INALCO?), 99 pp.
new_statements.locator: Part II 'Études antérieures, état des connaissances', A. Phonologie, §5 'Accent tonique', p. 26 (main quote); §3 'Tons', p. 24 (tone/stress interaction); B. Morphologie §1.4 Possessif (stress shift under suffixation); Syntaxe §3 Coréférence (enclitics never stressed)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (177,856 bytes; tag-stripped text of the saved 2023-02-01 Internet Archive copy of the academia.edu landing page, which embeds the full extracted memoir; twin also contains the passages). All four quoted passages are present verbatim: (1) lines 951-960, under the heading '5. Accent tonique' immediately after the in-text page marker '25' (TOC line 159: 'Accent tonique 26'): 'Dans les mots de deux syllabes ou plus, l'accent tonique tombe en règle générale sur la penultième. Lorsque celle-ci comporte une voyelle longue, l'accent tombe sur elle; si la voyelle est simple, l'accent se traduit par la gémination de la consonne suivante : si2ne2 "jaune" se prononce [si1nne2].' follow…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (penult: penultimate stress); adds the phonetic correlates (long vowel or gemination of the post-tonic consonant), the tone-stress interaction (three-tone language in which high tone tends to sit on the stressed syllable and detoned syllables lower), stress shift under possessive suffixation, and enclitics being unstressable. Opened via the the Internet Archive snapshot (2023-02-01) of the academia.edu landing page, which embeds the full extracted text of the memoir; the live academia.edu URL still returns an automated-access block (4th attempt, not reachable by automated download) and no PDF was obtained.
new_statements.rule_in_words: In words of two or more syllables stress falls regularly on the penultimate syllable (of the word including suffixes: adding a possessive suffix moves the stress rightward onto the new penult; enclitics are outside the stress domain and never stressed). Phonetic correlate: a long penult vowel carries the stress; a short stressed penult vowel triggers gemination of the following consonant (si2ne2 -> [si1nne2]; /ts/-type consonants 'redouble'). The language also has three lexical/grammatical tones (high, mid, low); high tone very often coincides with the stressed syllable and a syllable that loses stress under suffixation lowers its tone (ta1že1 'his father-in-law' vs ta2ža1na1 'my father-in-law'). The description is explicitly a point-by-point restatement of Veerman-Leichsenring (2000), Gramática del chocho de Santa Catarina Ocotlán.
new_statements.exceptions: 'en règle générale' (as a general rule) — no specific lexical exceptions listed; monosyllables exist (e.g. a2 'or', classifier u2-); the numeral ngu2 'one' used as indefinite article is unstressed; enclitic coreferential pronouns never take stress; stress shifts to the new penult when possessive suffixes are added (with shortening of the preceding vowel).
new_statements.identity_note: The memoir explicitly describes the variety of Santa Catarina Ocotlán (following Veerman-Leichsenring's 1996 fieldwork there), i.e. exactly choc1279; §6 lists phonetic differences from the Natívitas, Tulancingo and Teotongo varieties but says nothing about stress differing between them.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim on the page scan we hold of Mock 1977 p. 25; it is the entire accent statement in the book (scanned search of all 154 held pages). (2) The deciding source is a 1977 ALIM questionnaire sketch by a professional linguist, held in full; the classification (penultimate default, weight-blind, lexically marked exceptions incl. final stress) follows directly from it. (3) A newer and fuller description exists and is not yet obtained: Veerman-Leichsenring's 2000 reference grammar of the same village variety (xiii+140 pp), plus her IJAL 2000 pp. 321-322 stress discussion; neither is open access. sources.quote: No statement of stress position for Chocho. Says stress is contrastive/penultimate in Metzontla Popoloc (Veerman-Leichsenring 1991: 36-38: '(CV)CVCV pattern with stress on the penultimate vowel') and that 'Veerman-Leichsenring (2000b: 321-322) argues that Popoloc, Chocho, and Ixcatec also have stress in monosyllabic words, phonetically realized as vowel gemination, disyllabic realization of a diphthong or through the addition of an affix as a prothetic vowel.' Mazatec stress final.
